title: The Man in El Paso
logline: Ted's red cowboy boots end up on the shelf of a Ninth Avenue thrift store, and the shy Foley artist who buys them for eleven dollars becomes the coolest man in New York overnight. While Ted learns the boots were never the problem, Marshall sweats out a guilty secret that isn't his, and Barney bets Robin he can out-cool a man who barely talks.
coldOpen: Kids, in the spring of 2013, a total stranger bought my red cowboy boots for eleven dollars. Within a week, he was the coolest man in New York.

couch.line: Dad. You're wearing them right now.

guests.name: Lyle Oberholtzer
guests.role: a painfully shy Foley artist who makes the footstep sounds in movies; speaks softly in as few words as possible, hears everything, judges people by how they sound, and was invisible his whole life until eleven dollars of red boots made his silence look like mystery

guests.name: Irene Szabo
guests.role: owner of Second Chances Thrift on Ninth Avenue since 1981; prices every donation by how sad its donor looked handing it over, never forgets a donor's face, and announces prices like verdicts

scenes.summary: Ted, twenty minutes from a date with a stained-glass restorer, can't find his boots. They live by the door. Lily cuts off the man in El Paso. Ted leaves in sneakers. Marshall realizes he dropped four donation bags at the thrift store on Ninth that morning, and the bags were by the door too. Flashback: Irene prices his Fiero sweater by grief. Lily votes to never tell Ted. Button: the mall Santa.

beats.line: It started on a Saturday night, twenty minutes before a date with a woman who restored stained glass.
Has anyone seen my boots? They live by the door. They've lived by the door for nine years.
Which boots?
The red ones, Marshall. You helped me name them.
Maybe they finally left you. Everybody has a limit.
My date restores stained glass, Lily. She respects craftsmanship. Those boots were hand-stitched in El Paso by a man named—
Ted. You've mentioned that man more times than you've mentioned your own father.
My father never hand-tooled a pull strap.
Whoever moved them, I will find out. I once noticed a doorknob was a quarter inch low. In a hotel. In Belgium.
Great. Great skill. Very normal. Have a wonderful date. Bye now.
I have to wear sneakers. She's going to think I'm a man with no story.
Ted. That's the dream.
Lily. The donation bags.
What about them?
This morning I took four bags to the thrift store on Ninth. The bags were by the door.
Lily, the boots live by the door!
Oh, Marshmallow. What did you do?
I don't know! I wasn't thinking! I was saying goodbye to my Fiero sweater!
Baby. Did you cry at the thrift store?
A tasteful amount.
It's a sweater with my old Fiero on it. My mom knitted it in 1998.
The Fiero's dead. The sweater shrank. I'm the only one of us left.
Forty dollars.
Forty? It has a hole in the armpit.
I price by grief. You wept. Forty dollars.
Leave the bags. Take a tissue. Tissues are a dollar.
We have to tell him. Tonight. The second he walks in.
Absolutely. Or, hear me out. Never.
Those boots have been on every bad date Ted's had for nine years. This is a gift. To women.
Lily, I can't keep secrets from Ted. I told him about his own surprise party. In the cab. On the way to it.
How are you so calm about this?
I'm a very calm person, Marshall.
You bit a mall Santa.
He knew what he did.

scenes.summary: Two days later Ted is in mourning; Barney is throwing a parade. A shy man in Ted's boots boards and every woman in the car looks up. He's Lyle, a Foley artist who heard the boots across the store at Second Chances and paid eleven dollars. Since Saturday: cabs stop, landlords flirt, he got promoted to lead footsteps on a Western. He turns down five hundred dollars and a house. Ted decides he was ahead of his time. Barney bets Robin he can out-cool Lyle; the loser sits through Ted's director's cut of the boot story.

beats.line: Two days later, I was in mourning. Your Uncle Barney had a different word for it.
Ted, buddy, I'm so sorry for your loss. I'm also throwing a parade.
I've called two shoe repair shops, the lost and found at Penn Station, and a psychic.
What did the psychic say?
That they're with a better man now.
Barney. Every woman in this car just looked up from her phone.
Obviously. I'm in this car.
Those are my boots.
Excuse me. Sir. Those are my boots.
No. They're my boots. Second Chances, on Ninth. Saturday. Eleven dollars.
Eleven dollars?
Left toe, scuff shaped like Ohio. I'd know them anywhere.
I know. The left heel clicks on the downbeat. The right one sighs. I heard them from across the store.
Hi. Ted Mosby, architect.
Lyle. Footsteps.
Footsteps?
I'm a Foley artist. I make the sounds in movies. I do feet.
Whenever somebody walks in a movie, somewhere, I'm walking.
Lyle. Why is this entire car staring at you?
It's been like this since Saturday. A cab stopped for me. I wasn't hailing. I was stretching.
Four women gave me their numbers. One was my landlord. She fixed my sink.
And I got promoted. Lead footsteps on a Western. My boss says I walk like a man with a past.
I don't have a past. I have a cat.
Lyle, I'll give you a hundred dollars for them.
No, thank you.
Three hundred.
No, thank you.
Five hundred, and I'll design you a house. With a mudroom. For the boots.
No, thank you.
Thirty-eight years, nobody saw me. Yesterday a stranger said I have kind eyes. Same eyes.
This is me.
Do you know what this means? The boots were always cool. For nine years, I was ahead of my time.
That's one theory.
Please. He's a quiet man in loud shoes. I could out-cool that guy in my sleep.
Bet you can't. Loser sits through Ted's full story about the boots.
The director's cut?
Ted. Are there slides?
No.
There are four slides.
Challenge accepted.

scenes.summary: Ted invites Lyle to MacLaren's to negotiate. Marshall interrogates Lyle about where he bought the boots and panics. Wendy compliments the boots and comps Lyle's beer. Lyle's whole technique: he says thank you, then nothing. The gang shuts down the man in El Paso; Robin's flashback proves the boots work for four seconds, until Ted opens his mouth. Ted accepts that he's the problem; Lily intercepts Marshall's confession. Barney arrives in white ostrich boots from Milan; Lyle hears the squeak; Barney's silence lasts four seconds. Lyle leaves to escape a neighbor's screenplay, and Robin reveals she gave him her number. Ted decides Lyle should keep the boots. Button: Robin quacks.

beats.line: That Wednesday, I invited Lyle to MacLaren's. Strictly to negotiate.
So, Lyle. Where exactly did you get the boots? Just curious. For no legal reason.
Second Chances. On Ninth.
Ninth? Never been. Never heard of it. Don't know a Ninth.
He's scared of Ninth Avenue. There's a pigeon.
Love the boots.
Thank you.
Your beer's on the house. Obviously.
On the house? I wore those boots in here for nine years. She asked if I sang in a barbershop quartet.
Lyle. When people ask about the boots, what do you say?
Thank you.
And then?
Then nothing.
Nothing? No welt construction? No history of the pull strap? No man in El Paso?
There's a man in El Paso?
Oh, Lyle. There's a man in El Paso.
No!
Ted, the boots were never the problem. I dated you in those boots.
And these? Hand-stitched in El Paso. By a man named—
Ted. It's been forty minutes. I ate your bread.
You're right. I'm sorry. Let's talk about you.
So. The heel.
Those boots work, Ted. For about four seconds.
It's true, buddy. The boots walk in and the room goes, ooh. Then you explain them, and the room goes, oh.
So it's me. For nine years, I was the problem.
Ted, I have to tell you something. The reason your boots—
—look so good is your confidence. That's what he was going to say.
Lily. He's in pain.
He's in sneakers. He'll live.
Lyle. Ladies. Ted. Daddy's home.
Are you wearing cowboy boots?
White ostrich. Custom made in Milan.
They make cowboy boots in Milan?
They do now. I paid them to.
Your left heel squeaks.
It does not.
Like a duck that just got bad news.
Fine. You want the strong silent type? Daddy can do silent.
So last night I'm at this club in Tribeca, and the bouncer goes—
Four seconds.
I should go. A woman in my building wants to tell me about her screenplay.
Everyone tells me things now. I used to hear the whole city. Now I just hear screenplays.
He fled. That's a forfeit. I win.
I gave him my number.
You're the judge!
He didn't explain a single thing all night. It was like a spa.
Then Lyle should keep them. Somebody should wear them right.
For the record, my heel does not squeak.
Quack.

scenes.summary: Second Chances Thrift. Ted came to find a second pair; Marshall came to steer him to Brooklyn. Irene recognizes the crier, and Marshall confesses with a nine-page letter, but Irene corrects him: the boots came Sunday, alone, carried by a tiny redhead who skipped. Eleven dollars. Lily was protecting the women of New York. Lyle arrives with the boots in a box, miserable; Irene prices them at four hundred dollars. Lyle asks why Ted bought them, and Ted finally tells the real story without the stitching. Lyle hands them over; he already recorded the left heel for the Western. Barney and Robin arrive to settle the bet; Robin cancels Friday with a bootless Lyle. Barney demands the man in El Paso; Ted just says they're boots, and it's cool. Then Irene charges him four hundred dollars.

beats.line: This is where Lyle found them. Maybe there's another pair. Boots come in pairs, Marshall. Maybe pairs come in pairs.
Or we try a different thrift store. In Brooklyn. Or Ohio.
You. The crier.
You know Marshall?
Saturday. Four bags and a Fiero sweater. I put the sweater in the window. People stop and weep.
Ted, I did it! I donated your boots! The bags were by the door, the boots were by the door, and I'm a monster!
I wrote you a letter. It's nine pages. There's a poem.
No.
No?
He brought sweaters. The boots came that afternoon. Alone. Carried in by a tiny redhead.
She skipped. Thirty years, I've never seen a donor so happy. Eleven dollars.
Lily?
Lilypad! You let me sweat for a week!
You sweat so cute when you're guilty.
Why?
Ted, I have watched you explain those boots to sixty women. Sixty. I was protecting the women of New York.
Hi. I'd like to donate these.
Four hundred dollars.
Four hundred? You sold them to him for eleven!
Look at his face. That man is devastated.
Lyle. Why?
I miss being nobody. Nobody talks to nobody. I could hear the whole city.
This week I heard eleven screenplays. Four were about a detective who is also a dog.
Keep them, Lyle. You wear them right. You never explain them.
Why did you buy them?
I was twenty-eight. I walked past them in a shop window in Austin four times.
Everything I'd ever done, I had a reason for. Five-year plans. Pro and con lists. For sandwiches.
The fifth time, I went in. No reason. I just wanted to be a guy who wears red boots.
I explain them because I'm scared someone will laugh before I finish. They're the bravest thing I own.
Then stop finishing.
Ted, that was beautiful. I still hate them.
Besides, I recorded them. Your left heel is in a Western next fall.
I'm the sheriff?
You're the sheriff's feet.
Still squeaks.
Lyle. Hey. Still on for Friday?
Yes.
Wearing the boots?
No.
I have a thing Friday.
Okay, Ted. I lost. Let's get it over with. Tell me about the man in El Paso.
Nah. They're just boots.
Oh no. That was cool.
No! I've been dreading this for a week! Who is the man in El Paso?
Sir. Four hundred dollars.
Can I explain?
No.
That fall, a movie sheriff walked into a saloon on my left heel. And I never explained the boots again.
Dad. You've been explaining them for twenty minutes.
His name was Esteban, kids. He had a garage in El Paso and a dog with three legs.
